newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Little solace for U.S. tobacco in Latam.
newsitem.headline: Little solace for U.S. tobacco in Latam.

text.p: Latin America's army of carefree smokers may not offer much of a market opportunity for the U.S. tobacco industry's woes as it struggles to fend off ever increasing legal claims at home.

Even if Latin Americans puff more than most, industry officials doubt there is any room for U.S. cigarette makers to increase their already high presence in the region to make up for the loss of smokers in the United States as consumers turn ever more health conscious there.
It may be that "in restaurants here there seems to be a smoking section and a chain-smoking section," as Susan Wermcrantz, a tobacco industry analyst at Argentina's Banco Republica, said.
And Jorge Vives, president of Argentina's Chamber of Tobacco Industry, agrees health is not high on the list of concerns here but said: "In Latin America the industry faces other problems."
Among them is the mountain of contraband cigarettes that in some countries make up as much as half the market.
For instance, contraband Marlboro cigarettes are among the top brands in Colombia. Authorities say most of the booming trade is controlled by drug traffickers laundering illicit proceeds from abroad.
According to Santander Investment, contraband cigarettes hold an estimated 55 percent of the market in Colombia.
In Ecuador, of annual consumption of 170 million packs (each containing 20 cigarettes) some 60 million packs are estimated to be contraband.

"The average share of the market by contraband products is 35 percent in the majority of the provinces and there is a tendency of it rising to a much higher level than that if tax is not reduced," said Ana Maria Molina, the manager of corporate affairs at Ecuador's Tobacco, Drink and Foodstuffs Industry lobby.
Ecuador recently raised its so-called special consumption tax on cigarettes to 103 percent from 69 percent.

Although industry officials in some countries say there is room for U.S. companies to expand, foreign tobacconists already have a firm grip on several markets in the region, with foreign brands in many cases the most popular ones.
Phillip Morris Cos. Ltd. and Britain's B.A.T. Industries Plc have the longest reach in the area through association agreements or, as in many countries, outright ownership of local producers.

In Brazil for instance, a market worth $7.7 billion a year, cigarette maker Souza Cruz, which is 75 percent owned by BAT, makes seven of the top 10 brands with the remaining three made by Philip Morris. Souza Cruz' Derby alone holds a 40 percent market share.
In Argentina, Phillip Morris' Marlboro has 36 percent of the market.
BAT dominates nearly 90 percent of the market in Chile as well through its 70 percent stake in Chiletabacos, which makes top-selling brands including Belmont, Derby and Lucky Strike.

But with the high smoking rates in the region's larger countries that ranges from one-in-four to one-in-three adults, there are hordes of customers that producers eagerly hope will change their brand allegiance.
Tobacconists find few restrictions standing in their way. Huge billboards with tough outdoor types or Tom Cruise lookalikes adorn the skyscrapers of most Latin American cities.

Laws are stricter in some countries but in most places cigarette packets only carry a tame warning that "smoking is harmful to your health." In Brazil and Chile consumers are alerted that smoking causes cancer.

Advertising goes a lot farther than just billboards in some countries. In Venezuela and Argentina for example, young women promoters in mini-skirts often hand out sample cigarettes drinkers at trendy down-town bars.

In most countries cigarette advertisements cannot be aired on television until after 9 p.m. or 10 p.m. But that does not stop cigarette producers from hiring such high-profile personalities as Antonio Banderas.

An Argentine television advertisement has the smooth Spanish actor, hair swept back, dancing at a plush mansion with women and friends at an evening cocktail party by the poolside. "Exclusively Banderas, exclusively Parliament," says the voice-over.

Despite this, as economic reforms and high growth lead to increased wealth in Latin America, there are signs that health considerations and stricter controls on smoking and advertising may be in the offing.
